turn_text: Ranking member on the Ag Committee of Mr. Peterson of Minnesota said it's important to find a smart way to balance the consumer demand for information with what is known about the safety of foods that America's farmers produce. How is your legislation a balancing act to clarity?

I think that's exactly right. I think Mr. Peterson hit it on the head. You know, he's a Democrat, I'm a Republican. That's one of the things that's been frankly most appealing to me about working on this is we're working not along party lines here. So I'm excited that I think we can actually get this done. And he's right, you have to strike the balance. We've done a couple of things to do that. The first is, it is absolutely the case today. And if my bill were to become law, it would be the case the day after it did, that any food producer who wants to put a label on their food that says, my food contains no genetically engineered components or is non-GM. They still have the right to do so. So if you want to purchase organic food or non-GM food, go to the store, find products that are labeled that way, and purchase those for your family. You'll likely to pay a bit of a premium. But if that's the choice you make, I believe in markets and freedom, I'm a conservative Republican, and so I think that's great. The second thing we've done is we have now created, it wasn't in the bill last year, but we've created a USDA certification process similar to the USDA organic certification process that will permit food producers voluntarily to say, I want to submit my food, I'm going to have the USDA do a certification, And then I will have the USDA stamp of approval that says my food is, in fact, or my food product is, in fact, GMO free.

What has industry told you about the challenge of potentially having 48 different states with 48 different sets of rules? You've already had 30 states proposed and lots and lots of legislation. What's wrong with the patchwork approach?

Goodness, our founders understood that we were a nation of commerce and put in our Constitution, the Interstate Commerce Division, and it was aimed precisely at issues like this, where it's not really just about 48 states. There'll be cities and towns and counties that have their own ideas about what their labels ought to look like in their own community. And so you'll have literally could potentially have hundreds of different requirements, some of which would be conflicting. And to ask, especially small producers of food, some of the big guys might be able to figure that out. But small and medium-sized businesses that are trying to introduce products into the food stream who are required to put in hundreds of different levels couldn't possibly be expected to do that in a way that would be affordable for consumers. You know, I always think about it, like in Kansas, we make airplanes, and Learjet, and Babarti, and Cess, and all, all in my district. There are things that are intrinsically national in commerce and food labeling is one of those.
